title: Chapter 27: The Noise of a Name
paragraphs: It was so unnatural that for the first few seconds he just lay on the narrow bed in the room above the "Red Cauldron" and suspected the world of personal malice.

Behind the thin wall, someone was snoring as if trying to saw through their throat from the inside. From below came the smell of sour beer, burnt root, and old smoke. Somewhere in the corridor a lodger coughed, then spat for a long time into a wooden bucket. Agdash was not fully awake yet, but was already making sounds that promised: the day would be as dirty, noisy, and stubborn as yesterday.
His body ached after yesterday's encounter with Mask. Not badly. Not like after a real fight. More like the ache of something used for its purpose for the first time in a long while.
His fingers were intact. The knuckles ached slightly. A small blue spark lazily flickered between his index and middle fingers.
He didn't want to get up.
That was exactly why he got up.

He washed with cold water from a cracked jug, pulled on his patched jacket, checked his pockets, which held almost nothing useful, and left the room. On the stairs he nearly bumped into an elven maid carrying a bucket of ash.
She looked at him with sleepy eyes.
"I don't like it either," Anar replied.

Not dark, not light, but exactly gray, as if the world hadn't yet decided whether to show its face today. Low clouds hung over the upper terraces of Agdash. They didn't drift, they pressed down. Smoke already curled in the gaps between the roofs. Lava channels under the bridges glowed dimly, like poorly healed cuts in black stone.

The old training ground by the abandoned warehouses greeted him with silence. The dummy that had collapsed from lightning yesterday still lay by the wall in two charred pieces. Dust had settled overnight in an even layer. In the center of the stone circle was a blackened patch of old fire. Water crept along the edge of the low wall, seeping from somewhere above, although there had been no rain yet.
Then he looked at the sky.
"Of course," he said. "I got up before dawn, and the curtain-man decided to sleep in."
Anar put his hands in his pockets and began pacing in a circle. At first slowly. Then faster. Then he stopped because he realized it looked like he was nervous.

He had simply come on time to an unknown guy who had killed him three times in five minutes yesterday, promised to train him, didn't give his name, and left as if he were not a man but an unpleasant thought.
A distant thunder rolled in the sky.
On the warehouse roof stood a black figure.
He hadn't appeared. Hadn't come out. Hadn't climbed up.

Simply one moment the roof was empty, and the next Mask stood there, wrapped in layers of dark fabric. The cloak flapped behind him in the wind like a burnt banner. The gray dawn lay on the bandages, on the hilt of the curved blade, on the narrow slit where golden eyes dimly glowed beneath the fabric.
Then he stepped off the edge of the roof.

Anar had already opened his mouth to say something about suicidal habits, but Mask didn't fall. He slid down the wall, barely touching the ledges, caught a crack with his fingers, turned in the air, and gently landed on the ground.
Dust rose around his boots in a thin circle.
Anar looked at the roof. Then at him.
"You could have just come down the stairs."
Mask walked to the center of the ground and stopped.
Anar straightened up automatically. He expected words about stance, breathing, left foot, hands, shoulders, anything from yesterday's list of humiliations.

"Popularity," Mask repeated. "You want a tournament. A tournament is not a brawl. A brawl happens in an alley when two idiots argue over a coin, a woman, or a look that's too loud. A tournament is a stage. There they kill not only with weapons. They kill with a name."
Anar was silent for several seconds.
"I thought you'd teach me not to die."
"By making sure you're noticed the right way."

Thunder rolled over Agdash again. Somewhere above the first hammers were waking. The city entered the day heavily, with wheezing and clanging, like a sick giant ordered to carry walls on its back again.
Mask raised his hand and pointed to the arena hidden behind the warehouse walls.

"The weak get crushed there. The strong get feared. The unknown get forgotten. But the one whose name makes the crowd roar starts to be taken into account. Judges turn away more slowly. Scribes write more carefully. Opponents get angry early and make mistakes sooner. Rich idiots from the upper terraces start arguing whether to bet on you. Girls look longer."
"You need money, status, respect, and for people to stop looking at you like dirt on the wall. Those are honest desires. Not noble, not beautiful, but honest. You can work with honest desire."
Anar wanted to reply with a joke but didn't.
Not to save the world. Not great songs. Not frescoes where he stands with an outstretched hand against a shining sky. Although, to be honest, a fresco didn't sound bad either.
He wanted people to think of something other than a cell, an outsider, a lazy guy with no place who yells at the guards and then sits with an orc when they hear the name "Anar."
"But if you make every strike just to make someone gasp, you'll die."
"So you have to become popular but not think about popularity?"
"Stop thinking about what others will think," said Mask. "Make them think about what you decided to show."
Mask nodded as if silence was the right answer.
"Ah, so the left foot after all?"
So easy that Anar almost felt offended.

Mask didn't hit him, didn't throw him against walls, didn't demand he fall a hundred times and get up a hundred and first. He placed Anar in the center of the circle, adjusted his shoulders, nudged the left foot half a palm to the side with the tip of his boot, and made him just stand.
"Not like you're guilty. Like you're alive."
Anar raised his chin by the thickness of a finger.
Anar exhaled through his nose. Inhaled again. Slower.
After ten minutes his legs began to ache.
After twenty it became clear that standing correctly was harder than throwing lightning.

Mask didn't raise his voice. That annoyed him the most. He spoke evenly, dryly, briefly. One step. Turn. Inhale. Shoulder. Elbow. Don't look at the blade. Look at the chest. Don't pull mana into your fingers. Pass it through the body.

He had decided to be silent since the morning when he was going down the stairs. If he opened his mouth, he would start arguing. If he started arguing, Mask would say something precise. If Mask said something precise, the day would be ruined completely.
So Anar was silent and moved.
By the first hour of dawn he was already sweating.
By the second he realized the light training had been a lie. Not a direct lie. Worse. A lie that began as truth.

Mask added steps. Then turns. Then short bursts. Then made Anar launch a spark not from his fingers but from his feet, through his shins, thighs, stomach, chest, shoulders, and only then into his palms.
The second time the spark immediately broke off in his hands.
The third time Anar jerked his arm irritably, and the blue discharge slammed into the stone by the wall.
Mask silently looked at the crack.
Now he understood what Mask meant.

Mana was not water. It was not fire. It was not a wire. Words hardly fit at all. But if you didn't grab it, if you didn't try to squeeze it through your fingers right away, a path appeared inside. A thin, living line from the soles to the spine. From the spine to the shoulders. From the shoulders to the arms. It didn't want to be dragged. It wanted to be left alone.
A blue spark ran under his skin from heel to palm.

The rain hadn't started yet, but the air was filled with that metallic taste that awakened everything inside Anar. He raised his eyes to the sky. Between the warehouse roofs, clouds swelled like lead. At the edges of Agdash's upper tiers, protective lightning rods flashed - thin spires with copper rings driven into towers and bridges.

- The lightning inside you and the lightning above you speak a close language. Not the same, but close. If you pull it with your hands, it will strike wherever it wants. If you let it pass through your whole body, it will go through you like an open door.
- Because if you could die from that, I wouldn't waste my morning.
Anar wanted to clarify whether that was a compliment or an insult. He remained silent.
Someone appeared at the edge of the platform.
Stephanie stood by a low arch between the warehouses.

She wore a dark cloak, damp at the edges from the moisture. The reddish flame of her hair flickered with a faint, stubborn spark. She didn't step forward. She simply stopped in the shadows, saw Mask, saw Anar in the center of the circle, and froze.
Anar noticed her out of the corner of his eye.
His first impulse was to straighten up and look better.
The second - to do something impressive.
Mask struck his shoulder with a wooden training stick.
Not hard. Enough to bring him back into his body.
- You've already started performing for the audience.
Stephanie clearly didn't hear everything but understood enough. Her face grew more serious.
- The storm will arrive three heartbeats after the next flash. Stand still.
Now the training no longer seemed easy.
It didn't strike. For now, it only lit up from within like a huge gray carcass, in which bones briefly appeared. A second later thunder rolled, and the stone beneath his feet trembled.

- Next, - Mask said. - Don't catch it with your hand. Catch it with your body. Entering through the shoulders will kill your stance. Entering through the head will kill the meaning. Let it enter through the entire contour.
He raised his hands but didn't stretch them out. His fingers spread. His feet stood on the stone. The left one a little differently. That damned left leg.

The lightning tore from the sky not at him, but at the copper spire on the warehouse roof. In the ordinary world, it would have gone into metal, stone, earth. In Agdash, the ordinary world had long since worked only half the time.
For a moment he felt empty.
Not weak. Not broken. Just open.

A white discharge tore from the spire, curved like a living creature, and struck the platform beside him. The stone exploded into dust. Stephanie screamed. Anar didn't hear it. At that moment, all sound became light.

It passed through his soles, chest, teeth, eyes, spine, palms. Blue and white mixed beneath his skin. The hairs on his arms stood on end. The air around him smelled so thickly of storm that breathing became almost sweet.

He saw every crack in the stone. Every drop of water on the low wall. Stephanie's fingers clenched on the edge of her cloak. Mask's dark fabric fluttered not from the wind, but from the field around Anar.
And he also saw a figure on the upper gallery of the warehouse.
A huge silhouette stood under an arch, leaning on an axe.
At first Anar thought it was a statue.

It was a werewolf. Broad-shouldered, tall, with a gray mane of hair and a lazy, almost brazen posture. On his shoulder lay an axe so large it seemed made not for battle but for arguing with city gates. He looked at Anar without fear.
Later he would learn it was Djanavar.

Later he would hear how the arena called him the Gray Axe, the lone wolf of the Western Tract, a favorite of those spectators who preferred their fighters to have a simple philosophy: hit - problem gone.
Now Djanavar simply stood on the gallery and watched how the stranger from another world held a piece of the storm inside him.

The discharge flew from his palms not as a line, but as a wide, dazzling blue spear wrapped in white veins of real lightning. It struck a distant mannequin, passed through it, knocked down a weapon rack, burned a black circle on the wall, and disappeared somewhere in the stone depths of the warehouses.
The silence after the strike was almost indecent.
Stephanie looked at Anar as if she saw not a man, but the answer to a question she was afraid to ask.
Djanavar on the gallery slowly whistled.
- Lightning without a leash bites its master first, - he said from above in a hoarse voice.
Djanavar raised his free hand in a lazy greeting and disappeared into the passage.
Anar stood in the center of the circle, breathing heavily.
He wasn't staggered. Nothing hurt. On the contrary, his body felt full, light, too alive. He felt he could do it again. And again. And ten more times.

The guard. The workers by the notice. Those who looked at the stranger's jacket, the thin face, the lack of a sword, the lack of a place in the city. Even friends, perhaps, were simply used to seeing Anar as the one who lies around, jokes, gets angry, and never finishes anything.
Too much for the eyes that all this time decided who he was.
Anar wiped his wet brow with his sleeve. The first drops of rain finally began to fall on the platform, breaking into dark spots on the dust.
- I got the principle. Stance, flow, not with fingers but with the whole body. The storm is food. Very beautiful, very useful. I can go sign up now.
Stephanie looked away, as if she felt awkward witnessing a blow that hadn't landed on the body.
- I want to sign up while the table is open.
- The table will be open after training.
- You don't need a lecture, - Mask said. - You need the habit of not running away after the first success.
The rain intensified. Drops hissed on the heated pipes somewhere above. The platform darkened.
- I came on time, - he finally said.
- I did what you told me.
- I caught lightning from the sky.
- How many people in this city can do that?
- Fewer than those who can die from a knife in the side.
- You just don't know how to praise.
- I do. Avotu was right. The power in you is enormous. You're talented. You can become scarier than any fighter in this arena.
The praise came dryly, without warmth, without a smile. But it came.
And immediately after it, Mask added:
- And that's exactly why your irresponsibility is more dangerous than someone else's weakness.
Anar felt his face turn to stone.

- Sometimes one morning is enough. You want glory but don't want repetition. You want respect but get angry at scrutiny. You want money, status, girls, a name, but as soon as the work gets boring, you look for the door.

- I will, - Mask said. - You're not afraid of death as much as you're afraid of looking ridiculous. Public humiliation scares you more than a wound. That's why the crowd will hold you by the throat until you stop asking its permission to be strong.
It was foolish, fast, angry, and very honest.
Mask stepped aside half a step.

Anar flew past, turned, wanted to raise his hand, but Mask was already close. A palm pressed against his chest. A leg swept his knee. The world flipped, a stone hit his back, air flew out of his lungs.
The curved blade didn't leave its sheath.
Anar lay under the rain and looked at the gray sky between the roofs.
Stephanie was silent by the archway.
It was worse than if she had said something.
At first, Anar still got up. Not gracefully. Not heroically. Just got up because lying in the rain and looking defeated in front of Stephanie was unbearable.
They worked silently for another hour.
No storm. No spectators. No beautiful flashes. Step. Turn. Breath. Left foot. Short impulse. Release. Exit. Again.

Stephanie didn't leave immediately. She stood by the archway, then came closer but didn't intervene. The rain soaked her cloak, the flame of her hair lowered, thinned, but didn't go out. She wasn't watching the lightning. She watched the feet. The shoulders. How Anar repeated the same movement for the tenth time, though his face looked as if he was ready to insult the whole world by name.
When the training ended, Mask lifted his cloak from the low wall.
- If you say "impressive," I'll become unbearable, - Anar said.
Mask, passing by, barely nodded his head.
- She has better hearing than you.
- Today everyone decided to be helpful.
They walked to the arena together.
Halfway, Mask fell a step behind, then unexpectedly said:

Rain drummed on leather awnings, pipes, signs, stone steps. People hurried under arches, cursed, closed baskets, dragged children closer to the walls. No one noticed the black figure next to the stranger and the young fiery elf.
- Outside of us two, I'm Mask.
- You don't assemble a team from people who don't even know your name.
Anar digested this for several seconds.
They passed under a low gallery. Water dripped from above. Underfoot was a dirty mix of dust and ash.
- Tournaments are won by loners, - Utmysh said. - Glory is held by teams. One strong fighter becomes entertainment. Five strong fighters become a force to be reckoned with.
Anar wanted to smile. He couldn't. It sounded too serious.
- Because you have enormous hidden power. And because you're still foolish enough not to sell it to the first house that offers a nice room and a new jacket.
- You know how to spoil the pleasant.
Stephanie walked beside them silently. But Anar saw she was listening.
- Have you had a team before? - he asked.
Utmysh stopped so abruptly that Anar took two more steps before realizing.
Rain ran down the black fabric.
And that's why Anar understood: it would have been better if it had.

- At one tournament, the girl of one of us died. He decided the rest were to blame. Not the enemies. Not the arena. Not the rules. Us. Revenge was more convenient than grief. Then former allies began turning against each other. At first accidentally. Then no longer. Tournament after tournament. Blade after blade. In the end, only I remained.
- Since then, I haven't gathered a team.
- Now I need glory that won't die with one name. And I need people who can stand beside me without turning pain into a reason to cut their own.
For the first time that morning, the silence wasn't stubbornness.
Laren was indeed at the western table of the arena.

He sat under the awning, surrounded by wet lists, wooden boards, inkwells, and the expression of a man who already regretted his career choice. The old scribe wasn't there. The guard from yesterday wasn't there either. Instead, by the column stood a sleepy woman in a chainmail cloak, eating something from a clay bowl.
The tournament was approaching, and Agdash, it turned out, was full of people who had hands, legs, their own names, and an alarmingly weak attachment to life.

Two twins with identical braids argued in front of the table. Behind them stood a fat man with an iron club, which had more spikes than practical sense. Further on was a thin mage in a blue cloak, wet to the knees, and a woman with a spear decorated with red ribbons.
When Anar approached, Laren looked up.
It was obvious right away. Neither the fear of a legend, nor respect, nor the echo found in memory appeared on his face. Only tired bewilderment.
"The recording is still running. If you've come... calmly."
Laren didn't believe a single sound.
Utmysh placed a small black plate on the table.
It was the size of a coin, but not a coin. Matte metal, on one side - a thin engraving in the shape of a ring crossed by a diagonal line.
Laren took the plate and frowned.
"Then ask the senior scribe when he returns. For now, write."
Laren looked at the sleepy guard.
The moment turned out to be foolishly important.
He wanted the name to sound beautiful. Weighty. So everyone in line would turn around. So Stephanie would hear. So Mask - Utmysh - would understand: yes, he hadn't wasted his morning for nothing.
Stop thinking about what others will think.
Anar said in an ordinary voice:
"Is that a home, a city, a clan, or a disease?"
Laren stared at him for several seconds, then wrote: "foreign world." He looked as if hoping the paper would explain it to someone else.
"Yesterday you saw that it is indeed a weapon."
"I saw a breach of public order."
"Do you know the rules of the first stage?"
Laren was glad to have the chance to recite a text that required no personal opinion.

"The first stage is a general fight. All registered participants enter the field of the Great Arena. Magic is allowed. Any weapon, if the owner can bring it onto the field themselves or persuade someone to bring it before the signal. Patrons, bets, and fees are not counted in the first stage. After the signal, the fight continues until the number of active participants is reduced to one hundred. Defeat is counted upon surrender, loss of consciousness, stepping outside the outer circle, or inability to continue fighting as decided by the referees. Finishing off the unconscious is prohibited. Violations result in disqualification, fines, imprisonment, or execution, depending on the judges' mood."
Laren looked at him over the list.
"Accidental deaths in the arena happen often."
He handed Anar a tablet with wet clay.
Laren took the tablet and placed it next to the list.
The word was heavier than Anar expected.
Stephanie stood a little behind. Utmysh - nearby. The queue was noisy, cursing, moving. No one applauded. No one gasped. Even the clay figurines of fighters at the neighboring stall looked past.
And at that moment, Djanavar appeared in the square.

Now he was not a silhouette on the gallery, but a living mountain of muscles, fur, old scars, and lazy confidence. The axe lay on his shoulder. The crowd before the table parted not because he pushed through, but because it suddenly became easier for everyone to live at the edges.
"They say he took off a helmet with a single blow, head and all."
Djanavar approached the table, looked at Laren, and smiled broadly.
"The pen doesn't bite those who write fast."
Laren sighed as if the day had finally decided to become long.
"A name without scars is quickly forgotten. Djanavar."
The werewolf slightly raised the axe.
Djanavar turned his head to Anar.
His yellow eyes gleamed with amusement.
"Thunder in a cage still seeks the sky."
"The sky is wider in the arena."
The laughter was low, hoarse, without malice. But the people nearby still took another half step back.
He pressed his finger into the clay so hard the tablet cracked.
Anar looked at the huge axe.
"You choose people by the principle 'if he kills me beautifully, we take him'?"
Friends found out the same day.
Not because Anar made a solemn announcement. Solemn announcements required confidence, and confidence after the morning fall in the rain behaved unpredictably.
Simply, Ravan saw the clay registration mark on his wrist.

They sat in the evening in the corner of the 'Red Cauldron.' Below, workers made noise; it smelled of sour beer, hot oil, and cheap stew. Zhenya ate as if he had forgotten that food could be more than just fuel. Yura was counting some notes on a scrap of leather. Alexander listened to two elves at the next table and pretended not to listen. Avotu stood by the wall, black flame above his head flickering almost lazily. He looked as if conversations about local tournaments were happening far from the real problems of the world.
Stephanie, sitting at the edge of the table, silently stared into her mug.
Anar realized it was too late to hide it.
- I've signed up for the tournament.
Not completely. In the "Red Cauldron," complete silence could only fall in case of fire, murder, or free food distribution. But their corner truly froze.
Ravan was the first to speak:
He didn't say "you're an idiot." He didn't say "they'll kill you." He didn't say "you won't make it."
Yura exhaled and rubbed the bridge of his nose.

- Anar, it's a bad idea. Not "unpleasant," but logistically, medically, socially, and in every sense. There will be professional fighters. Locals. Those who have spent their lives breaking other people's bones.
- I have some now too. They killed me three times yesterday, once today.
Zhenya looked at him for a long time.
- I don't have gear for you. Everything I'm gathering now is tailored for Ravan and the mine guards. I can't put iron on your mana; it would only get in the way.
- I know. Just saying in advance so you don't stand in the workshop later with a face like "Zhenya, make me something so I don't die."
Alexander was silent longer than the others.
Anar wanted to answer quickly. It didn't come immediately.
- Not just because the guard offended you?
- I'm having an honesty day today.
- I don't see diplomatic risk. Agdash loves arenas, not our permits. If you're going anyway, it's better we know and are nearby.
- I didn't say it's smart. I said it's already happening.
Ravan leaned back against the bench, folding his arms.
- If they start killing you there, I'll step into the field.
- I care a little less, but still not enough.
The tension at the table shifted. It didn't disappear but stopped pressing directly on the chest.
Avotu, who had been silent until then, looked at Anar.
Anar waited several seconds for more.

Avotu clearly didn't care not because he didn't value Anar. It was just that in his mind, arenas, titles, fighter lists, and city rules were too small things compared to the sky that had once torn open and still hadn't healed.
- He's stronger than he looks, - she said.
- Is that supposed to be reassuring?
- But he doesn't just want to die beautifully. I saw the training.
He felt that unpleasant warmth under his skin. Public attention. But it wasn't a square, not a guard, not a crowd. These were his own.
He wanted to joke it off even more.
- Yes, - he said. - I need it.
Zhenya clinked his mug against his.
- Is this our official strategy now?
- It works more often than you think, - said Alexander.
Yura still looked like he wanted to schedule alarms, injuries, and possible funerals but raised his mug too.
Anar looked at them and understood: they considered it dangerous. Possibly foolish. Possibly a waste of time.
For the next seven days, Anar rose before dawn.
The first two days he was proud of himself.
On the third, he almost arrived late.
On the fourth, he tried to convince Utmysh that repeating the same movement two hundred times wasn't training but a form of local bureaucracy.
On the fifth, he abandoned the exercise halfway through because "the principle was clear," and was immediately pressed face-first into the wet dust.
On the sixth, he did the same without explanation because sometimes a person repeats mistakes not out of ignorance but out of character.
Step. Turn. Breath. Mana through the body. Not fingers. Not face. Not anger. Not the audience.

Stephanie didn't come every day. But when she did, she stood quietly. Sometimes she repeated movements without mana, off to the side, with a stubborn face. Anar saw this and for the first time didn't think about her weakness. She was weaker than him. Much weaker. She had no storm tearing into the sky, no huge reserve of strength, no feeling that the world could be forced to retreat if desired.
But she didn't abandon a movement halfway through.

The first time - on the upper gallery, with a piece of roasted meat in hand, as if he had come not to someone else's training but to a performance. The second time - below, by the wall. He said nothing. Just watched as Anar redirected short discharges between three iron rings without touching the wet rope suspended between them.
When the rope finally flared, Djanavar laughed.
- Smoke always brags about fire, - he said.
- But the audience would wake up.
- The audience wakes up even from a fire in the stable.
- A dry knife jokes quieter than a wet one.
- He's not a teacher, - said Anar.
By the seventh day, Anar had learned three things.
First: if you place your left foot correctly, the world really becomes a little less comfortable for those who want to hit you.
Second: the crowd starts watching even before the fight. Your walk, your silence, how you stand in line, how you hold your hands, how you react to laughter.
Utmysh said that was enough to survive the first stage.
Anar decided not to clarify the difference.
On the day of the tournament, Agdash became different.

People from all tiers of the city - and beyond - were streaming toward the Great Arena. Caravans arriving over the past days had brought fighters from southern fortresses, northern houses, ash camps, underground guilds, distant outposts that Anar had never even heard of. Fire elves in house colors walked the streets, people with skin the color of old bronze, dwarves in heavy breastplates, orcs, half-orcs, mages in travel cloaks, mercenaries, beastfolk, two translucent hydrolis, inside which neon blue lines flickered.
The world that seemed to be dying somehow found the strength to come and watch others die.

Food, amulets, cheap flags, participant lists, figurines of favorites, pain ointments, prayer ribbons, knives for self-defense, and knives called self-defense knives only because it sounded more decent were sold at the arena.
Agdash's power was present as well.

Representatives of the houses sat on the upper balconies. Below them - guild masters. Even lower - soldiers, workers, miners, merchants, children on adults' shoulders, old men pretending not to be interested though they had arrived first.
The tournament was not just entertainment.
The city roared because otherwise it would start tearing itself apart.
Anar stood in the participants' passageway and listened to that roar.
He expected it to be more terrifying.

The crowd was enormous. It lived as one body but with thousands of mouths. Its smell came in waves: sweat, meat, beer, wet fabric, hot stone, fear, excitement. Somewhere above, drums were beating. Referees in red-and-black cloaks walked the arena sand, checking the outer circles.
Black cloak, dark layers of fabric, face covered. Against the backdrop of colorful fighters, he looked almost too plain.
"Then why did you torture me with that lecture about popularity?"
"The first lesson was: stop thinking about what others will think."
"The arena does too. Get used to it."
Djanavar appeared at the other end of the passage.
The crowd noticed him even before he stepped out. His name spread through the stands like a strike on a drumskin.
He stepped onto the sand first among the favorites, raised his axe, and the arena answered with a roar.
He didn't need to prove his right to the noise.

Then the house fighters were announced. Red cloaks of the eastern house. Black-and-gold armbands of the southern terrace. Three brothers with identical curved swords. A mage in a blue cloak. A woman with a spear and red ribbons. A half-orc with a chain hammer who had nevertheless found a way to settle a family matter.
Anar's name was announced closer to the middle.
Some laughed. Some buzzed. Someone shouted:
"Show us where your world is, we'll send the trash there!"
Anar felt the first angry charge run through his fingers.
The charge retreated beneath his skin.
The first stage didn't resemble a fight.
It resembled a catastrophe given rules.

Hundreds of participants entered the field. Some immediately took the edge, some sought allies, some shouted threats, some prayed, some laughed too loudly. Referees climbed stone platforms at the edges. Red runes of the score flashed above the arena.
It's forbidden to finish off the unconscious.
Anar repeated the rules in his head until they almost became a rhythm.
The first ten seconds killed all plans.

Someone threw a fireball into the crowd at the center. A shield bearer next to Anar took a spear to the thigh and fell, immediately raising both hands. A woman with two blades slipped between three fighters and cut one's shoulder so cleanly the blood looked painted on. The half-orc with the chain hammer howled with delight and knocked down two at once.
The first attacker was a guy with a short axe. Fast, angry, too confident. He saw a skinny stranger without armor and decided it was an easy way to reduce the number of participants.
Anar looked not at the axe.
A blue charge struck the guy's chest - not hard, but precise. He twitched, dropped the axe, and fell to his knees, gasping.

Not like in training, where every stone was familiar and Utmysh stood nearby, dryly naming mistakes. Here everything moved at once. People screamed, fell, blocked views, smelled of sweat, iron, and fear. Someone shoved Anar with a shoulder, and he almost got hit by a foreign hammer. Someone hit him with an elbow on the cheekbone without even noticing.

The second and third attacked together. He blinded one with a flash near the face. Hit the other's knee with a low charge. The fourth turned out to be an earth mage and raised a stone slab before him. Anar almost struck it with all his strength but felt in time that it was a trap: the slab was wet with some black liquid.
The mage was surprised just enough to get the handle of his own staff in the stomach from a woman with a spear running past.
Anar didn't even understand how it started working.

Where the crowd of fighters would become denser. Where someone had already raised a sword too high. Where you shouldn't attack but remove yourself from someone else's attack. Where a wide charge was needed to scare, and where a thin one to disable a leg. Where you could win not by a strike, but by two others crashing into each other.
Then a house fighter in a red mask came at him.
He moved low, fast, with two short blades. Didn't shout. Didn't look at the lightning. Looked at the chest.
Anar realized the man was trained.
And almost immediately let a blow to the ribs through.
Not deadly. But enough to make the world narrower.
The blade slashed his jacket at the shoulder.
A little more - and the blood would have been deeper.
For a moment Anar didn't hear the arena.
He heard laughter at the western table. "To the people or to the mistakes of nature." He heard someone in the stands shouting that the alien would fall now. He heard his own heart.
Public humiliation rose hotter than blood in his throat.
He wanted to strike so hard that everyone would shut up.
The red mask saw it and retreated.
Anar was almost raising his hands to the sky.

The storm hadn't left yet. Clouds hung low, right above Agdash's ring. Protective spires on the upper terraces hummed with tension. He could take the lightning. Could show everyone. Could leave a glass circle on the sand and make the stands remember not the skinny jacket, not the alien world, not the laughter, but the light.
Then the red mask made a small shoulder movement.
Anar realized he wouldn't make it.
He did the only thing that didn't look graceful.

Didn't roll, didn't slip into a graceful low step, didn't turn the fall into a move. Just threw himself down into the sand like a sack. The blade passed over him. The red mask collided by inertia with the half-orc swinging a chain hammer. The hammer grazed the house fighter's shoulder, who cursed, turned, and within a second the red mask was fending off two opponents instead of one.
- The stranger buried himself in the sand!
Anar got up on all fours, got kicked in the back by someone's boot, cursed, and rolled back under the cover of a fallen shield.

The shield took the brunt of a stream of tiny icy needles that would have pierced his face. Anar, lying in the sand, struck the legs of the mage who had released those needles with a short burst. The mage collapsed, immediately raised his hand, and surrendered.
The sand clung to his wet jacket. There was dirt on his cheek. One sleeve hung like a torn rag. Somewhere in the fall he lost the lacing on his right boot, which now sloshed with every step.
Laughter came from the upper rows.
And instead of striking toward the stands, he dove behind the backs of two heavy shield bearers who were trying to push through the center.
Thus began his true first stage.
Anar hid not because he was weak.
He hid because there were too many strong ones in the arena.

He struck from the side when two were already locked together. He tripped with lightning the legs of those who swung too elegantly. He flashed light into the eyes not of the most dangerous, but of the one standing between him and a foreign blow. Once he fell himself, pretending to be hit by a wave of fire, and let three fighters pass over him, who immediately crashed into Djanavar.
Djanavar threw them off with his axe like a bad thought.
For a second his gaze found Anar in the sand.
He only said so quietly that Anar read it more from his lips than heard it:
And then he went back into the fight.
The runes above the arena blinked, counting the remaining active participants. One hundred fifty. One hundred thirty. One hundred fifteen.
The Red Mask was still holding on.

He had already knocked out three. Escaped the chain hammer. Cut the strap on a foreign shield. Pushed a wounded opponent toward the referees without finishing him off. The crowd began chanting his house sigil. He was the one people bought seats in the arena for: fast, precise, spectacular, almost noble.
The Red Mask was fighting a woman with a spear near the outer circle. She was strong but tired. One more exchange - and he would have knocked her out. A score rune flashed nearby.
Anar stood behind the Red Mask, in a dirty jacket, with sand on his face and a boot that betrayed him with every squelch.
Step back and wait for an honest end.

A thin blue pulse passed over the sand, hit the Red Mask under the knee, and for a moment disabled the leg. That was enough. The woman with the spear, not understanding what had happened, pushed him with the shaft in the chest. The house fighter lost balance, stepped back, and crossed the outer circle with both heels.
For a second the arena did not understand.
- Such are not allowed in the second stage!

The Red Mask stood beyond the outer circle, breathing heavily. He was not wounded. Had not lost consciousness. Had not surrendered. He simply lost by a rule everyone knew and almost no one liked when it concerned the crowd favorite.
The woman with the spear looked at Anar as if undecided whether to thank him or strike him.
Anar stood in the sand, among the groaning, cursing, surrendering, and celebrating, and understood: his name was now known.
Only pronounced as if they wanted to spit it out.
Utmysh approached him from the edge of the field.
- They're shouting that I'm not worthy.
- You passed the stage, - said Utmysh. - And lost to the arena.
- You stand and listen as they decide who you are.
Because again it was exactly right.
The conference before the second stage took place in a stone hall beneath the eastern stand.
Only the passed participants, arena representatives, scribes, referees, several important guests, and those who could look like they had the right to be anywhere were allowed in.

A hundred passed fighters stood or sat in groups. Djanavar sprawled by a column, resting his axe across his knees. The woman with the spear was bandaging her arm. The mage in the blue cloak glared angrily at the wet edges of his clothes. The house fighters kept apart. The Red Mask sat on a bench, pale but alive, and did not take his eyes off Anar.
At the far table, the referees prepared the draw for the second stage.
Shouts from outside still pierced through the stone.
- Cowards have no place in the second round!
Every time the crowd chanted, someone in the hall looked at Anar.
Anar stood next to Utmysh and was silent.

He wanted to go outside and show them once again. Wanted to say that the rules did not forbid falling, retreating, striking from the side, and moving on if you were still standing in the circle. Wanted to ask where they were when Djanavar threw people with his axe so that sand flew three rows back. Wanted to send them all away at once, preferably with a good formulation.
- It's about to start, - he said.
Utmysh raised his hands to the bandages on his face.
- You said no one should know.
- I said you had enough. The stage is over.
Utmysh untied the first dark ribbon.
One of the senior referees raised his head.
Utmysh removed the cloth from his face.
Under the mask was not a demon, not a ghost, not a monster.

A harsh face with sharp cheekbones, short dark stubble, old scars near the lips and on the bridge of the nose. Eyes - golden, calm, tired. No mysticism. No legendary glow. Just a man who had survived too long where others turned into names on walls.
The first to recognize him was not Laren.
Laren, sitting by the wall with the protocols, only frowned.
The first to recognize him was the old referee at the draw table.
He stood up so abruptly that the chair struck the stone floor.

He didn't shout immediately. At first, it was exactly a breakdown: conversations stopped, heads turned, some didn't understand, some understood all too well, someone whispered the name to their neighbor, and the name spread through the hall faster than fire across dry cloth.
Djanavar slowly rose by the column.
For the first time, there was no lazy smile on his face.
Anar stood next to the man who had been tending to his left leg for seven days, beating his shoulder with a stick and telling him not to quit halfway.
And only now did he realize that for the others in the room, the man standing beside him was not a scheduling problem.
Next to him stood the legend of the arena.
Utmysh placed the removed mask on the table before the arbiters.
Laren dropped the folder with the protocols.
